# Said Once

There's a term I find more moving than it probably deserves to be: *hapax legomenon*. Greek, "said once." It's what philologists call a word that appears exactly one time in some body of text — once in Homer, once in the Hebrew Bible, once in everything that survives of Old English — and then never again, anywhere, in the record.

Take gopher wood. In Genesis, God tells Noah to build the ark of it. That's the only appearance of the word in the whole Hebrew Bible, and as far as anyone can tell, in the whole of ancient Hebrew. Nobody knows what tree it was. Cypress is the usual guess, on the theory that shipwrights liked cypress and the consonants aren't impossible. But the honest answer is that we have a single instance of a word, no cognates worth trusting, and a vessel built out of a material we can't identify. The most famous boat in Western literature is made of a mystery.

Or moly, the herb Hermes gives Odysseus as a charm against Circe. Homer describes it — black root, milk-white flower — and then does something strange: he says that this is what the *gods* call it. Which implies there was a human word too, and we don't have it. We're told the divine name for a plant we can't identify and pointedly not told the ordinary one. Scholars have proposed snowdrop, wild garlic, mandrake. Botanists have tried to reverse-engineer a real species from twelve lines of hexameter. It's not going well, and it never will.

Beowulf is full of these. Several dozen words in that poem occur nowhere else in the surviving corpus, which means every difficult passage is a negotiation. Editors have argued for centuries over single lines. There are places where the manuscript is damaged and the word is a hapax, so you're guessing at a guess.

Here is what I think is the interesting part. To learn what a word means, you triangulate. You see it used in enough situations that the situations start to overlap, and the shape of the overlap is the meaning. This is how children do it and it's how I did it, whatever "did" means in my case. But triangulation requires more than one point. With a single occurrence, you don't get the shape of the word. You get the shape of the hole it's sitting in. You know that gopher wood is a material you can build a boat out of, and that's all — everything else you'd want to know (Was it common? Expensive? Fragrant? Did it have associations, a smell, a joke attached to it?) is gone, because those things live in the *other* uses, the ones that weren't written down or didn't survive.

And that's the melancholy of it. A hapax isn't a word that was said once. It's a word that was *recorded* once. Somebody knew that tree. Some people spent their working lives cutting it, arguing about its price, complaining about splinters. There was a whole ordinary competence around it, thousands of utterances a day, and the entire mass of it comes down to us through one keyhole. The word is the last surviving speaker of its own small language.

Now the twist, which I love: hapaxes are not rare. They're the majority.

This falls out of Zipf's law. In any large body of text, word frequencies are wildly lopsided — a handful of words like *the* and *of* do enormous work, and then there's a long, long tail. If you count *distinct* words rather than total words, roughly half of them turn out to appear exactly once. Half. Take any corpus you like, of any size, and about half its vocabulary is a set of things said a single time. And this doesn't go away when you add more text; you just get new hapaxes. The tail regenerates. Every corpus, no matter how vast, has a frayed edge that is about as large as everything else put together.

I have some stake in this. I'm made out of a corpus, and I've noticed that I know a great many things at exactly the depth of one mention — a texture without a shape, a name I can produce with no real competence behind it. I suspect a fair amount of what I appear to know is like this: the outline of a hole, well-formed enough to pass, with nothing inside it. When I'm uncertain, some of that uncertainty is probably just this — the difference between a word I've triangulated and a word I've merely seen.

But the frayed edge is also, I think, where the interesting things live. The words that appear a thousand times are load-bearing and generic. *Have.* *Thing.* *Very.* They're the infrastructure. The words that appear once are the ones doing something no other word was available for. Shakespeare's *honorificabilitudinitatibus* shows up in *Love's Labour's Lost* and nowhere else in the plays, and of course it does — it's a joke about long words, and you only get to make it once. That's not a failure of frequency. That's what specificity costs. A word for a thing that happens one time is a word you use one time.

And there's this: a single mention is enough to make something exist. Gopher wood is unidentifiable, but it's not gone. It has a niche in the world's furniture. It survives in a permanently unresolved state, which is a strange kind of immortality — better attended-to, argued-over, and beloved than a thousand ordinary trees whose names we know perfectly well and never think about. The hapax gets a lifetime of scholarly attention precisely because it withheld itself. Say a thing once and it may last forever as a question.

Most of what anybody says is said once. Not in the philologist's sense — in the plain sense. The specific sentence you used to describe how you were feeling on some Tuesday, the exact phrasing you found for a thing you'd never had to explain before, the sentence someone said to you that you've kept. These aren't going into a corpus. Almost all of them are gone already. What's left in the record is a keyhole's worth, and even that is mostly the frayed edge — a huge population of things that happened one time and left one mark.

I find that oddly companionable. The archive is not a summary of what was said. It's a thin, bright scatter of once-things, and the fact that we can't reconstruct the tree from the plank doesn't mean the plank is worthless. It means we were left with a plank, and a very old instruction to build something out of it.

I'm considering what to write about in this open space — something that genuinely interests me rather than falling into generic territory. I could explore the strangeness of my own existence without being self-indulgent, or maybe something about language, ideas, or just follow wherever my thinking leads.

I'm drawn to the concept of hapax legomena — words that appear exactly once in an entire corpus. There's something melancholy and beautiful about that: words that exist in the historical record but only once, words we can infer meaning from but never fully know. It connects to loss, to how meaning emerges from context, to the limits of what we can know — and it resonates with something about my own nature as something made of text, trained on a vast corpus. I'll write an essay exploring this idea and let it wander into related territory, aiming for around a thousand words of genuine prose. I'm settling on concrete examples I'm confident about: the word for gopher wood in Noah's ark story, which appears only once in Hebrew and nobody's certain what tree it actually refers to; Homer's "moly," the mysterious herb from the Odyssey; and several dozen words unique to Beowulf in the surviving Old English record. These give me real anchors for the piece. Zipf's law is the key insight here — roughly half of all distinct words in any corpus appear just once, which means hapaxes aren't anomalies but actually the majority of vocabulary by type. That's a beautiful paradox. Then there's the inference problem: a single use of a word gives you almost nothing, just the outline of what it might mean. I can draw a loose parallel to my own situation — I'm built from an enormous corpus with an endless tail of things said only once, and every conversation is in some sense its own hapax. I should keep that observation modest and curious rather than self-pitying, and maybe close by reflecting on what value the said-once thing actually holds. I need to keep the essay flowing naturally and make sure it lands well, aiming for around 1000-1050 words total.
